A bench does not move. But it can help a person keep moving. For an older adult, a long walk can become several shorter steps. There is time to stop, sit, and rest before walking again. A study in 3 neighboring areas of Vancouver listened to adults aged 60 and older. Researchers used seated interviews and walk-along talks. They met 28 participants in 2012 and 22 in 2014. The older adults said benches helped them enjoy green spaces and places by the water. The seats gave them rest during walks. They also supported short talks and a feeling of connection. The researchers described this with a warm image: Benches become like porches. A porch is between private life and public life. A neighborhood bench can play a similar role. A 2023 review gives a wider view. It studied 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. The review reported that older park users preferred more benches, linked to their wish to relax.

Parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, cafés, and good care were also reported to encourage older visitors.

But public space can move in the opposite direction.

Some benches are tilted or divided by middle armrests. Other benches are removed. When such changes are used to stop sleeping or other activities, they are called “hostile architecture” or “defensive design.”

In 2021, an NYC Transit social media post said subway benches were being removed to stop homeless people from sleeping on them. The post was later deleted. The MTA said it had been posted in error. It was not proof of an official removal policy.

So, the bench debate is not only about street furniture. It is about who can rest, who can stay, and how easily older adults can move through their community.
A bench is a small object, but it can open or close a city. A place to sit can also be a place to keep moving—and to stay connected.

Benches also helped them enjoy green areas and waterfront spaces. But the role of a bench did not end there. The study described how benches can become like porches. They are neither fully private nor fully social. They create a simple place where neighbors can stop, talk, or just spend time near one another. A 2023 review added a wider view. It examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. The review reported that older park users preferred more benches, linked to their desire to relax. Other literature in the review said that well-kept parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, and cafés encouraged older visitors.

At the same time, some public benches have been changed to limit how people use them. Sloped seats and center armrests can prevent people from lying across a bench. In other cases, benches are removed completely. These choices are often discussed as hostile architecture or defensive architecture. This creates a difficult question: Is a bench only a seat—or is it part of someone's ability to move through the city? A design that blocks one activity may also remove a resting place for someone else. Yet the evidence about the wider harm remains limited. As of March 2020, one article reported that no wide-scale empirical study had measured the effects of hostile architecture on homeless people or other targeted groups.

A bench may be a small piece of city furniture, but it can serve as a rest stop, a neighborhood porch, or a signal that some people should move on. How cities design the pause helps shape who can remain in public space.

The quiet problem starts after the shopping is done. Fruit and vegetables go into the refrigerator. They may look safe inside the crisper drawer. But that drawer may have a small slider or dial. It is not just decoration. Many refrigerators offer 2 settings: high humidity and low humidity. Each setting has a different job. High humidity keeps the drawer more closed. This helps hold water around the food. It is useful for vegetables, especially leafy greens. These vegetables lose water quickly. When that happens, they become dry and wilt.

Low humidity allows more air to move through the drawer. This is important for fruit. As fruit becomes ripe, it gives off a natural gas called ethylene. If this gas stays around other fruit and vegetables, they may become ripe too quickly. Then they can go bad sooner. A low-humidity drawer lets the gas escape more easily. This can help the food around the fruit last longer. So the basic rule is simple: Fruit usually goes in low humidity. Vegetables, especially leafy greens, usually go in high humidity. It is a small change. But it gives each type of food the environment it needs.
Give leafy greens a closed, humid space, and give fruit an open path for its gas. The right drawer can mean less wilting, slower spoilage, and produce that stays useful for longer.
